title: Ezekiel 16:44–52
context: The LORD extends the allegory with a proverb, “As is the mother, so is her daughter,” and introduces Jerusalem's sisters: Samaria to the north (the left hand) and Sodom to the south (the right hand). Samaria had already fallen to Assyria (2 Kings 17:6), and Sodom had been destroyed (Genesis 19:24). The LORD names Sodom's sin as pride, plenty, careless ease, and neglect of the poor and needy, along with arrogance and abomination. Shockingly, he declares that Jerusalem has done worse than both, so that by comparison her sisters appear righteous. Ezekiel 23 develops a similar picture of Samaria and Jerusalem.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Behold, everyone who uses proverbs will use this proverb against you, saying, ‘As is the mother, so is her daughter.’
verses.arminianNotes: “everyone who uses proverbs will use this proverb against you.” Arminian readers see Jerusalem's conduct becoming a byword: “As is the mother, so is her daughter.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the proverb connects Jerusalem with the Canaanite origins of verse 3. Despite the LORD's kindness, she had returned to the ways of the land's former peoples.

verses.text: You are the daughter of your mother, who loathes her husband and her children; and you are the sister of your sisters, who loathed their husbands and their children. Your mother was a Hittite, and your father an Amorite.
verses.arminianNotes: “You are the daughter of your mother.” Arminian readers see the family picture showing a pattern of loathing husband and children, repeated in Jerusalem's betrayal of the LORD and sacrifice of her children.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repetition, “Your mother was a Hittite, and your father an Amorite.” The language is moral rather than genealogical, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: Your elder sister is Samaria, who dwells at your left hand, she and her daughters; and your younger sister, who dwells at your right hand, is Sodom with her daughters.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your elder sister is Samaria.” Arminian readers see Jerusalem placed in a family with Samaria to the north and Sodom to the south, both judged for their sins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that “left hand” and “right hand” reflect directions when facing east. Samaria is called the elder sister, perhaps because of its size, though the text does not explain the order.

verses.text: Yet you have not walked in their ways, nor done their abominations; but soon you were more corrupt than they in all your ways.
verses.arminianNotes: “Yet you have not walked in their ways.” Arminian readers see the LORD saying that Jerusalem did not merely copy her sisters but quickly became “more corrupt than they in all your ways.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the force of the comparison. Jerusalem, with greater privilege, fell further. Both traditions see that greater light brings greater responsibility.

verses.text: As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “Sodom your sister has not done, she nor her daughters, as you have done, you and your daughters.
verses.arminianNotes: “As I live,” says the Lord GOD. Arminian readers see the LORD's oath that “Sodom your sister has not done” as Jerusalem has done, a startling verdict meant to shatter her complacency.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Isaiah 1:10, which addresses Jerusalem's leaders as “you rulers of Sodom!” The comparison with Sodom was a familiar prophetic warning. These notes name the parallel without merging them.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Behold, this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and prosperous ease was in her and in her daughters. She also didn’t strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom.” Arminian readers see the LORD naming pride, “fullness of bread,” and “prosperous ease,” along with failure to “strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse lists the attitudes behind Sodom's sin, and verse 50 adds “committed abomination before me.” Both traditions read the two verses together rather than setting one against the other.

verses.text: They were arrogant and committed abomination before me. Therefore I took them away when I saw it.
verses.arminianNotes: “They were arrogant and committed abomination before me.” Arminian readers see the LORD's judgment on Sodom as a response to arrogance and abomination: “Therefore I took them away when I saw it.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Genesis 19:24 records how “the LORD rained on Sodom” sulfur and fire. Ezekiel recalls that judgment to warn Jerusalem, which both traditions treat as the point.

verses.text: Samaria hasn’t committed half of your sins; but you have multiplied your abominations more than they, and have justified your sisters by all your abominations which you have done.
verses.arminianNotes: “Samaria hasn’t committed half of your sins.” Arminian readers see the LORD's verdict that Jerusalem's sins were so great that she “justified your sisters,” making them look righteous by comparison.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samaria had already been taken into exile (2 Kings 17:6). Jerusalem had seen that judgment and still sinned more, which deepens her guilt.

verses.text: You also bear your own shame yourself, in that you have given judgment for your sisters; through your sins that you have committed more abominable than they, they are more righteous than you. Yes, be also confounded, and bear your shame, in that you have justified your sisters.
verses.arminianNotes: “You also bear your own shame yourself.” Arminian readers see Jerusalem, who once judged her sisters, now having to “bear your shame” because her sins were worse than theirs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase “they are more righteous than you,” which is comparative, not a declaration of innocence. Both traditions see a warning against self-righteous judgment of others.
